title: The harm of slander
hookLine: slandering the holy spoils the slanderer's own life (Sukhmani 13)

lines: WHAT IS THIS DOING TO US?
cards: A group chat, late at night. Someone posts a screenshot of a coworker's message and adds an eye-roll. Within a minute there are six replies.
Everyone has a story. Nobody is lying exactly, but by the end the coworker is a joke, and the chat has never been livelier. It feels good, in a sour sort of way.
You go to sleep a little buzzed and a little worse. Guru Arjan spends an entire ashtpadi on that buzz, asking the one question the group chat never does: what is this doing to us?

teach.b: The thirteenth ashtpadi is built like a drumbeat.
Line after line opens with the same three words: sant kai dookhan, through harming the holy, through speaking ill of them. Then each line names a cost. Life is cut short.
All peace goes. The mind becomes dirty. Honor is lost.
No one comes to help. The list runs stanza after stanza, the opening words returning like a knock on a door.
Now look at who pays, in every single line. Not the sant.
The good person being slandered never suffers in these stanzas.
The losses all fall on the slanderer: their peace, their mind, their standing, their life. That's the surprise, and it turns the group chat upside down.
We gossip because it seems to cost the other person something and give us something: a laugh, a bond, a bit of height. Sukhmani says the accounts run the other way.
The one being talked about loses very little; the one talking is the one being emptied. Two words to hold. Dookhan: speaking ill, finding fault, doing harm with words.

And nindaa, slander, the salok's own word. Even so, the first stanza leaves a door open: if the merciful saint shows mercy, even the slanderer is carried across in the saints' company. And why the holy, especially?
Because nearness to the good lifts us, and slander pushes the good away on purpose, and with them the very company that might have carried us across.

how: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib move through the thirteenth ashtpadi's repeated lines beginning sant kai dookhan, and nindaa, slander, is warned against in many hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib.

o: a curse that falls on the one spoken of
honest criticism given to help someone

games.q: the harm of slander — tap the pairs.
p: through speaking ill of the holy

s: in the thirteenth ashtpadi, the slandered saint suffers most
every cost in the stanzas falls on the slanderer.
many lines of the thirteenth ashtpadi begin with the same words
sant kai dookhan returns again and again, like a drumbeat.
the ashtpadi treats slander as a small, harmless habit
it lists cost after cost: peace, mind, honor, life.

games.q: the group chat is roasting a kind coworker. by the thirteenth ashtpadi, who loses the most?
games.why: line after line, Sukhmani says the slanderer pays: their peace, their mind, their honor. the good person loses very little.

practice: Sit and let the mind do what it does, and when it brings up someone who annoys you and starts a little commentary, don't argue with it.
Just stop the sentence halfway, like lifting a needle off a record, breathe out, and wait for the next one. You're not forcing kindness yet; you're only learning where the needle is.

wordCard.voice: Nindaa, slander. Sant kai dookhan, speaking ill of the good: in the thirteenth ashtpadi, line after line, the one who speaks is the one who pays.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: nindaa, slander, speaking ill of someone; the word used in the salok.

carryVoice: Your line: slander harms the slanderer. The one talking is the one who pays. Four hundred eighty-seven days, and counting.

sources.ref: Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 13, stanzas 1–3 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 279–280)
